comparedAgainst: Top web results for 'C# arrays and List<T> dynamic array' (Medium/GeeksforGeeks/TutorialsPoint) seen in the results list; the Medium page returned 403 and was not read
justification: Far deeper than the best existing pages. Microsoft Learn's List<T> page never mentions memory layout, cache locality, insertion cost or growth policy, and the arrays reference has no measurements. This article measures the locality effect, demonstrates the layout with Unsafe.ByteOffset, cites ECMA-335 I.8.9.1 (I extracted the PDF: 'Array elements shall be laid out within the array object in row-major order' is verbatim, and the same paragraph mentions 'platform-specific padding', which supports the Sample[] claim), and its List.cs details all check out against dotnet/runtime (fields, indexer uint trick and comment, DefaultCapacity 4, doubling, Remove = IndexOf + RemoveAt, GrowForInsertion, IsReferenceOrContainsReferences clearing, _version increments including the indexer setter, MoveNext version check). Drepper section numbers (3.2 for 64-byte lines and the 3/14/240 table, 3.3.1 associativity, 3.3.2 sequential/random) are right. Doc quotes for Insert, RemoveAt, RemoveAll, Span<T>, ArraySegment<T>, CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan and the C# array reference all check out. run-code passes. I re-ran the traversal, grid, container and RemoveAt/RemoveAll programs: ratios and orderings reproduce. Held to 7.0 by one factual error (the RemoveAt 'exactly the number of elements that move' claim is off by one and contradicts the article's own bullet) and, separately, by the central cache explanation, which is stated as fact for the 2000-4000 range using the wrong quantity (whole-grid size instead of per-column reuse distance), omits the TLB (which Drepper himself flags as a major slowdown source in the paper cited), and gives a jagged-array mechanism that is not quite right. Without the error cap this would sit near 8.0; with the explanation fixed and a validating experiment it could reach 8.5.

issues.location: 'What Insert and RemoveAt really move', paragraph after Figure 2: 'RemoveAt is more precise: O(n) "where n is (Count - index)", which is exactly the number of elements that move.'
issues.problem: Factual error (off by one). RemoveAt(index) moves Count - index - 1 elements; the documentation's (Count - index) counts the removed element too and is an asymptotic bound, not an element-move count. The article's own first bullet says RemoveAt(Count - 1) moves nothing, but Count - index = 1 there. Insert is different: it does move exactly Count - index, as Figure 2 shows. The sentence applies the Insert count to RemoveAt.
issues.fixLooksLike: Quote the doc's O(n) with n = Count - index, then state exact move counts separately: Insert moves Count - index elements, RemoveAt moves Count - index - 1 (zero at the last index). Or drop 'exactly' and say 'about the number of elements after the index'.

issues.location: 'Why the column-first loop falls off a cliff', the paragraph beginning 'Apply that to each part of the table', and the three numbered facts
issues.problem: The central explanation reasons about the wrong quantity. It ties the column-first slowdown to the whole grid no longer fitting in the 16 MB cache. But a column-first pass revisits the same cache lines on the next column (16 consecutive columns share each line), so what matters is the reuse distance: one column touches n lines, about 250 KB at n = 4000, and that is never compared with L1/L2 sizes. So 'most of those lines have been evicted since the previous column touched them' is asserted, not derived, and 250 KB would fit in the L2 of many desktop parts. The TLB is never mentioned: a 16,000-byte stride lands on a new 4 KB page on every read, so one column touches about 4,000 pages, beyond typical L1 and L2 TLB reach, which fits the growth from 3.4x to 6x between 2000 and 4000. Drepper, the article's cited source, calls TLB misses 'another big reason for the slowdown' (section 3.3.2, detailed in his section 4). Only the 4096 effect is hedged; the 2000-4000 story is stated as fact.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add the per-column footprint arithmetic (n lines x 64 B) next to L1/L2/L3 sizes, add page/TLB reach as a second mechanism, and hedge the 2000-4000 mechanisms as consistent-with unless measured. Better, add a cheap validating experiment in the article's own style: pad the row length (4097 ints, a non-power-of-two stride) or tile the column-first loop in 16-column blocks, and show the cliff disappears. That also gives the reader the practical remedy, which the article currently lacks.

issues.location: 'Grids' section, paragraph 'Column-first, the jagged array is the worst by a factor of two...'
issues.problem: An unmeasured mechanism is stated as fact and is slightly wrong: 'each step touches two unrelated cache lines instead of one.' The outer array of 4,000 row references is read sequentially (8 references per line), so that read is nearly free of misses. The plausible extra cost is the dependent load of the row object (its Length for the bounds check, then the element), which the JIT cannot hoist per row inside the inner loop. This is the one place the page states a hardware cause without hedging or measurement.
issues.fixLooksLike: State what is measured (about 2.2x slower than flat and rectangular column-first) and offer the mechanism as a hypothesis: an extra dependent load from a different object per access, with the reference array itself read sequentially. Or add a variant that hoists the row (int[] row = g[r]) and measure it, which tests the explanation directly.

issues.problem: Drepper's 3 / 14 / 240 cycle table is what 'Intel lists for a Pentium M' (end of section 3.2); his sequential measurement is on a different processor (a P4) and shows about 4-9 cycles per element, not 'a few'. 'For the processor he measured' merges the two. Random access reaching 450+ cycles makes 'hundreds' fine.
issues.fixLooksLike: Write 'the Pentium M figures Intel lists, quoted by Drepper' and give the sequential number as roughly 4 to 9 cycles per element in his own test.

issues.location: First results paragraph ('Row-first costs about the same per element at every size') and the size-100 table row
issues.problem: The smallest grid, which fits in L1 and should be fastest, is the slowest row-first cell (1.16 ns against 0.73-0.89; 1.12 on my re-run). Column-first is equally slow there, which points to JIT tiering, not cache: each method gets a single warm-up call and size 100 is measured first. 'Flat from 40 KB to 64 MB' is therefore not quite true and the anomaly is unexplained.
issues.fixLooksLike: Warm up properly (repeat calls or disable tiered compilation via #:property) and re-measure, or call the size-100 cell a warm-up artifact and say what 'about the same' means (0.7 to 0.9 ns from size 500 up).

issues.location: 'One block of memory...': 'and the reason indices start at 0: the index is the distance from the first element.'
issues.problem: An unsourced causal claim about why languages index from 0. It is a common rationale, but history and convention are involved, and the brief forbids unsourced 'why' claims.
issues.fixLooksLike: Scope it ('which is why 0-based indexing gives the simplest formula') or drop the causal claim.

issues.location: Rectangular vs jagged results: 'g[r, c] on a rectangular array produced slower code here'
issues.problem: A missed chance to explain from a source already cited. ECMA-335 I.8.9.1 says arrays have lower and upper bounds per dimension, so a general multidimensional access accounts for lower bounds and checks each dimension. That is a likely reason; the reader is told only 're-measure'.
issues.fixLooksLike: One hedged sentence: multidimensional arrays carry per-dimension lower bounds in the CLI model, which the JIT must account for on each access, unlike single-dimension zero-based arrays.

issues.location: Span/ArraySegment section: 'accepts an array, a span or a segment without overloads, because implicit conversions exist from each.' and 'its remaining reason to exist'
issues.problem: The ArraySegment-to-ReadOnlySpan conversion is uncited (it does compile and run, also under LangVersion 13, so it is true, but the cited pages do not show it). 'Remaining reason to exist' overstates: ArraySegment<T> also implements IList<T>/IReadOnlyList<T> and appears in older buffer APIs.
issues.fixLooksLike: Cite the conversion or say 'the conversions exist (the program below relies on them)'. Change 'remaining reason' to 'the main reason to choose it over Span<T>'.

issues.location: 'What Insert and RemoveAt really move', bullet 1: 'At the end of the list, both are cheap: Insert(Count, x) ... move nothing.'
issues.problem: Insert(Count, x) moves nothing but can trigger the O(n) regrowth copy when the list is full; it is amortized O(1), not unconditionally cheap.
issues.fixLooksLike: 'Insert(Count, x) shifts nothing (it is Add, amortized O(1)) and RemoveAt(Count - 1) shifts nothing.'

issues.problem: Several things a reader of 'array vs list in C#' meets are missing: the cost of search (Contains/IndexOf O(n); BinarySearch on sorted data O(log n) and its precondition), a compact cost table for array vs list (index, append, insert, remove, search), array covariance (string[] assigned to object[] and the ArrayTypeMismatchException on store), and the List<struct> indexer pitfall (list[i].Field = x, CS1612). The brief requires every named operation to get its cost; search appears only as a component of Remove.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add a small cost table (with assumptions) to 'Picking between an array, a list and a view', plus one short paragraph or exercise on covariance or the struct-in-list trap. Do not lengthen the cache material.

issues.location: Exercise 'Measure what one cache line buys'
issues.problem: The prompt states the expected outcome ('should cost almost as much as updating every element') before asking the reader to predict it, which gives the exercise away (brief: do not give away exercises).
issues.fixLooksLike: Ask 'How should the time change as k grows from 1 to 64? Sketch the shape before running,' and move the cache-line reasoning into the solution.
